posts.title: Chinese Jokes in the New Era
posts.excerpt: People Really Do Laugh in Hell
posts.text: People Really Do Laugh in Hell 1: An Old Man Calls for Help An old man fell into a river and shouted for help, but the police ignored him. The old man changed his tune and shouted,“Down with the Communist Party!”Two police officers immediately jumped in, pulled him out, then gagged him and handcuffed him. 2: A Call from the Commission for Discipline Inspection The Commission for Discipline Inspection called all bureau chiefs to say,“Please come to the Commission tomorrow.”The result: the Land and Resources Bureau chief suffered a heart attack; the Finance Bureau chief turned himself in that very night; the Transportation Bureau chief fled to Canada; and the Health Bureau chief committed suicide by poisoning. A young Commission member sighed,“I just said one simple thing.” 3: An Official’s Son Visits in Prison After a certain official was placed under“shuanggui”(double regulation), his son visited him in prison and cried,“Dad, I just graduated from college and can’t find a job…” The official wrote a note to his son saying,“Take this to my former subordinates.”The son worried,“What good is writing a note now?! The official patted his chest and assured him,“Don’t worry. When I was in power, I could make whoever I wanted an official. Now that I’m inside, I can make whoever I want come in here.” 4: Differences Between Chinese and Foreign Fairy Tales Foreign fairy tales usually begin with“Once upon a time,”while Chinese fairy tales start with:“By the end of 2030, within the next five years, or thirty years from now.” 5: Mineral Reserves Antimony is a metal with the chemical symbol Sb (which sounds like the Chinese slang term for“idiot”: Shabi). China is one of the earliest countries in the world to have discovered and utilized antimony. China accounts for more than half of the world’s currently proven antimony reserves. After the founding of the People’s Republic of China, large-scale exploration and development of antimony took place. Currently, China ranks first in the world in both antimony reserves and production. 6: Flag-Raising at the Temple After the founding of the People’s Republic of China, an elderly monk led the monks at his Buddhist temple in a national flag-raising ceremony for the first time. A young novice monk, unfamiliar with the practice, asked the elderly monk,“Why do we need to raise the flag every day before eating vegetarian meals and chanting the Buddha’s name?”The elderly monk replied solemnly,“Because without the Communist Party, there would be no Tathāgata—the infinitely holy Buddha of great compassion and mercy, Communism!”

posts.title: Reflections on July
posts.excerpt: July is almost over, and I’ve temporarily escaped the grind of college life. As graduation approached, I wrote a reflection
posts.text: July is almost over, and I’ve temporarily escaped the grind of college life. As graduation approached, I wrote a reflection —back when I was still in the middle of my graduate school entrance exam interviews. Now that everything is over, I’ve been accepted into graduate school and have already left campus. After returning to campus in April, I spent every day relaxing in my dorm room—though “relaxing” was really just an excuse to indulge myself. Even though my final project wasn’t quite finished, I knew it was almost done, so I’d just lie in bed playing with my phone. In the evenings, I’d usually buy a bottle of soda and start eating and drinking to my heart’s content. But when I thought about all the hardships I’d endured over the past few years, drinking soda felt like a form of comfort. Sometimes, when I thought about the final project I was working on, I’d open my coding software and write some code. No one was really worried about failing the thesis—and there was indeed no need to worry, since we all knew what the school was like. Without a doubt, those few months were the most carefree time of our college lives. So, during the Labor Day holiday in early May, a few of us guys wanted to get away and discussed where to spend our vacation. After some back-and-forth with my roommates, the three of us decided to head to Qingdao for a few days. It was our first time at the beach—I’m from Jiangxi, and the other two are from Henan. As three kids from inland areas, our long-held dream of seeing the ocean finally came true. From Rizhao in Shandong to Qingdao, we stayed in a small hotel in a county town; after all, at 430 per person, that’s what we could afford. We headed to Qingdao the next day. I took a long-distance bus—the ride took several hours, and the bus was filled with college students just like us. We figured it was probably everyone’s first time seeing the ocean, and the beauty of the sea was truly breathtaking and captivating, especially on the Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, where the sight of the city surrounded by the sea left a lasting impression on me. As we entered the bustling city center, Qingdao gradually came into view. However, that day wasn’t exactly pleasant—we got up at 6 a.m. to set off and didn’t arrive until 10 a.m. We got off the bus right by the seaside, near the Zhanqiao Pier, a popular Instagrammable spot. I got tired after just a few steps; the aftermath of my indulgence significantly slowed my pace as I explored Qingdao. Afterward, we visited Xiao Qingdao, the Underwater World, the First Seawater Bathing Beach, Badaguan, and Zhongshan Park. By the time we reached Zhongshan Park, it was already 6:00 p.m. Finding a place for lunch had been a challenge, so I settled for a noodle shop next to the beach—I’d originally planned to have a seafood buffet, but the place was already packed at noon. While walking, I tripped over a round stone pillar and stumbled—a classic Chinese slip-up, if you will—which was one of the major disappointments of this trip. To us, Qingdao felt enormous; there was simply too much to see in one day. With so many attractions, we called it a day at Zhongshan Park. My friends and I decided to head back, feeling a bit regretful—it’s true that you can’t really see much in just one day. In early June, it was time to submit the first draft of our thesis. I’d already finished my graduation project, so I didn’t feel any pressure. We went through the defense—it was just a formality; basically, you just showed up and passed. Professors wouldn’t intentionally make students delay graduation. Two weeks later, the university held the graduation ceremony. We received our diplomas and certificates, and that was that. After three years of the pandemic, it’s been tough to even find a job—it’s driven everyone crazy—but we’ll keep moving forward. The Class of ‘23 really couldn’t have had it any worse. There were six of us in our dorm; four took the graduate school entrance exam, and I was the only one who got in. Those who didn’t make it are preparing to try again next year. Of the other two, one signed a tripartite employment agreement and started working, while the other just coasted through graduation and went home to try to land a job. And just like that, our college dorm life came to an end, and we all went our separate ways—north, south, east, west, and center. In late July, I received my admission letter from graduate school, but I wasn’t happy about it. I don’t like campus life—it’s stifling and dull. Most importantly, I’m broke. Financial pressures have been pushing me to start working and earning money as soon as possible, and I’m really anxious. Plus, as a student, I can’t help but face all kinds of judgmental stares. I want to stand on my own two feet, think for myself, and make my own choices. I want a stable environment where I can truly relax—and I want to see the world out there! I can’t let my life go to waste any longer!

posts.text: When I first decided to take the graduate school entrance exam, I didn’t really know why I had to do it. Deep down, I thought to myself: If I get into graduate school, I’ll have a better advantage in the future. My reasoning was very simple. During the nearly year-long preparation process, I felt physically and mentally exhausted—it was practically torture. My daily routine was a monotonous cycle between home, the library, and my dorm; I spent most of my time sitting on a bench reading and studying, relying only on listening to music and fantasizing about a so-called“bright future”to keep myself going. I finally stopped studying right before the exam and completely gave up on myself. I barely touched a book during the exam period. There were special circumstances then—the school had ordered us to quarantine. Originally, everyone was supposed to go home to quarantine and then return for the exam, but everyone in my dorm got infected with COVID-19, and on the day of the exam, I had a fever and a headache. It didn’t matter anymore. With only two or three days left, I had no heart to study; I just wanted to go home as soon as possible. As I sat on the train heading home, watching the trees rush by outside the window, I realized just how incredibly difficult this past year had been. It was just like the 2022 Qatar World Cup: Messi led Argentina to the World Cup final, while I was frantically working through math problems. Each of us was striving desperately toward our goals, giving it our all. In the end, Argentina won, but I didn’t know if I had won. Is life really just a competition or a game? Looking back on my four years of college, I entered university half-awake, bringing my past ignorance and naivety with me. I floundered this way and that but never found that “passion” the big shots always talked about. Maybe the campus was too small, or perhaps it was because my abilities and resources were limited. I spent most of my college years in a daze. During that time, I did try to break free from mediocrity—I took the CET-4 and CET-6 exams along with everyone else—but what’s the point of passing them? Now that I’m a junior, I’ve fallen into a different kind of confusion: Should I apply for graduate school? There are all kinds of opinions online—some say applying for grad school is a turning point in life; others say it’s a way to avoid graduation and entering the workforce; still others say it’s for a better future self, or that it’s a way to improve oneself. I don’t understand what exactly I’m supposed to be improving—my blood pressure and weight? Or my susceptibility to being deceived? If it’s just for the degree, forget it. To be honest, I do admire those classmates who worked hard to get into graduate school. Online, it’s mostly about prestigious universities. Whenever I see videos of students from non-985 and non-211 schools pulling off an underdog victory against 985 and 211 institutions, I feel even more lost. I don’t know what it’s all for—I’m just following others’ paths and plodding along step by step, without ever listening to what my heart truly wants. So this past year has been incredibly painful—carrying books back and forth, not returning to the dorm until past 10 p.m., always running away from something. I’m not sure what it is. Since entering college, I suddenly felt as if I’d been set free—much more independent and unrestricted—and that’s exactly why I’ve been so lost. No one ever introduced me to college life, and no one told us what we were supposed to do in college. There are plenty of online guides, though, covering every aspect of life, all laid out clearly and in detail. Graduation is just around the corner, and I’m still just as at a loss as ever. Between preparing for my final project, potential graduate school entrance exams, and job hunting, I can’t possibly handle everything. That’s just how life is—there are gains and losses—and I’m ready to face whatever the outcome may be. Maybe I don’t really care about the final result; I suppose I just like the feeling of reaping a small reward after putting in the effort. It can be pretty disheartening when you put in the work but don’t get anything in return. If I get into graduate school as I hope, will that make up for the slacking off and confusion of these past few years in college? I’ve fallen back into a state of “confusion.” I’m in graduate school now, poring over academic papers and writing code every day. My advisor might only reach out once a week. Once I graduate, I won’t know how to face life ahead, how to fit into this unfamiliar society, or how to survive in this world. It’s as if the university has built a thick wall to shield us inside—it seems I’ve merely switched schools only to continue feeling lost. When I was filling out my college application, I chose computer science out of mere curiosity. I hadn’t had much opportunity to interact with computers before college, and it wasn’t until I was hit with a barrage of tedious courses that I truly got my start in the field. After that, my knowledge remained largely theoretical; the most practical use I got out of it was playing video games with classmates—so I suppose I also got my start in computer games during my undergraduate years. Perhaps it’s time that pushes us forward, until we come to understand ourselves and begin to accept reality: I’m just a“pre-programmed person,”destined to receive an education and then enter the workforce—otherwise, how could I be called a programmer? Being a programmer isn’t so bad. Now that I’m nearing the end of my university’s journey, I don’t have to worry about not having enough money for food, shelter, and daily expenses. My mind is much more at ease and peaceful—perhaps I’m no longer lost. Of course, buying a house might be a problem, but it’s better than being unemployed and living off my parents. At least I have a stable income to support my family. There will be plenty of worries down the road, so I won’t dwell on daydreams anymore. In any case, I’ll just let things take their natural course. Parents want their children to make something of themselves, but this is just who I am. Do they even know the pressure we’re under these days? Young people are working their hearts out, all just to buy a place to call home in the city of their choice. Although my exam scores aren’t out yet, the final thesis and corporate spring recruitment have already begun. It’s time to leave this confusion behind and set out on a path that brings me peace of mind. These past few years of the pandemic have been really tough—it’s been so hard!

posts.text: Earlier, rumors circulated online that a young ByteDance employee, Mr. Wu, had passed away. A notice on ByteDance’s internal network stated that the company had been informed by the hospital that Mr. Wu had unfortunately passed away. The sequence of events was roughly as follows: At 6:00 p.m. on February 21, 28-year-old Mr. Wu entered ByteDance’s gym. After exercising for about an hour, he began to feel dizzy, and his condition worsened. Around 7:30 p.m. that evening, emergency medical personnel arrived on the scene, treated him, and transported him to the hospital in an ambulance. At 12:30 a.m. on February 23, the hospital reported that the employee was in critical condition. Shortly thereafter, Mr. Wu passed away. Speaking of this, I, too, initially applied to a computer-related major out of curiosity, which led me to a school I wasn’t particularly satisfied with afterward. At 28, he could be called a “senior”—a few years older than me—but his life was still so young! Senior Wu held a degree from a prestigious university and had long aspired to work in the IT industry. After graduating, he joined ByteDance and worked diligently; he got married, bought a home, published a book, and just a few months ago, his wife gave birth to their child. It’s hard to imagine that such a young senior—who should have gone on to lead a happier and more fulfilling life—would be taken from us so suddenly by such a cruel reality. Judging from Senior Wu’s social media accounts and current reports, he was a dreamer, lively and cheerful, and highly capable—he even owned a home, albeit with a mortgage. Despite the hospital’s best efforts to save him, they were unable to save his life. Wu’s passing has placed immense pressure on his wife. She plans to sell their home and return to her small county town to raise their child with her mother’s help. Regarding this news, I feel saddened and a sense of regret over Wu’s passing—regret that he was someone who deserved better from life, yet met such a tragic end; I also feel lost as a software engineering major myself, as I’m torn between finding a job and preparing for graduate school; I’m now questioning whether I should continue studying computer science or enter a related field. I also feel a mix of concern and relief for my fellow students majoring in computer-related fields or those about to enter the industry—relief that we still have our health and our lives, and relief that we still have some choices. Senior Wu’s passing is not an isolated case; another 26-year-old has also trended on social media. A designer at a Shanghai-based design firm reportedly died suddenly in his rented apartment early on the 15th, allegedly due to excessive overtime. The news of these two young people’s deaths coming so close together has had a particularly profound impact. Is this really the reality of life? Everyone knows that overtime is widespread in the IT industry, where work pressure and life pressures are both intense, and most professionals live in big cities. It’s understood that companies like ByteDance prefer highly self-disciplined individuals; they generally offer generous benefits, including free meals and beverages, a free gym, social insurance, and housing fund contributions. In such an environment, it’s hard not to strive for advancement, and even when you get home, you’re constantly studying. In short, the IT industry can be summed up in one word: “cutthroat competition”! Due to a widespread societal perception that the industry offers high salaries, the competition isn’t limited to the job search—it has even spilled over into the college entrance exams and graduate school applications. Everyone is rushing to major in computer-related fields, even switching majors, all with the sole goal of securing a high-paying job in the future. Yet, as the number of applicants continues to rise, even expanded enrollment quotas can’t keep up with demand, making the competition increasingly fierce. It’s not that other industries aren’t competitive—it’s just that the computer science field has become so intensely cutthroat that it’s off the charts! Regardless of whether a major is a good fit or if one is actually capable of doing the work, people are flooding into this trend—especially since the rise of artificial intelligence. At the same time, working at a major company like ByteDance today allows you to freely enjoy various generous benefits, but you’ll also feel a kind of “restricted freedom.” Despite flexible work arrangements, employees must complete various tasks; working alongside outstanding colleagues can help you excel, but you also have to endure the hard work and exhaustion. This isn’t to say people shouldn’t strive for success, but rather to consider what it brings them. If we overlook long-term benefits and the harm caused by forced overwork, even the strongest giants will eventually fall. When I saw the news about Senior Wu, I was deeply moved and wondered why such misfortune had befallen him. While it’s difficult to determine whether his sudden death was linked to overtime work, we should reflect on how to keep both the tech giant ByteDance and its employees thriving amidst such intense life pressures.
